issues.legal_issue: A writ court should not adjudicate a private dispute over competing property titles that requires proof of basic facts when no public-law issue or reviewable defect in the authority’s sale process is raised.
material_facts: The property had been mortgaged to secure a loan, and the original owner later transferred it through successive sales while the mortgage remained in place.

After default, the finance corporation took possession and sold the property under its statutory power; the purchaser paid the full offered price, and the corporation confirmed the sale, although no sale deed was executed.

The later purchaser sought cancellation of the corporation’s sale, transfer of the property to him, and restoration of possession, relying on his purchase and claiming lack of knowledge of the mortgage and sale.

Deciding the competing claims required determination of title and proof of basic facts; the writ petition did not challenge the corporation’s authority or the sale process for lack of jurisdiction or abuse of authority.
The High Court cancelled the sale and directed repayment to the corporation’s purchaser, thereby deciding the parties’ competing rights.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have determined the competing title claims in the writ proceeding and should have left the parties to seek remedies before a competent civil forum. The appeals were allowed and the High Court’s order was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226, a writ proceeding is not an appropriate forum to adjudicate a dispute whose essence is the parties’ competing private-law claims to property and which requires proof of basic facts, absent an issue arising from a public-law function. Even where a statutory authority’s sale is questioned, the writ court’s role is at most judicial review of the administrative action; it does not determine inter se private rights where the authority’s jurisdiction or the sale process is not challenged for lack of jurisdiction or abuse of authority. The Court relied on Godavari Sugar Mills Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra (2011) 2 SCC 439, para 8(vi), and Kisan Sahkari Chini Mills Ltd. v. Vardan Linkers (2008) 12 SCC 500, para 23.

rule.if: writ_proceeding and competing_private_property_titles and requires_proof_of_basic_facts and not public_law_issue and not authority_or_sale_process_challenged_for_jurisdiction_or_abuse

predicates.writ_proceeding: A party brought the dispute to court by a writ proceeding.
predicates.competing_private_property_titles: The parties asserted competing private claims to ownership or rights in the same property.
predicates.requires_proof_of_basic_facts: Resolving the competing claims required proof of basic facts.
predicates.public_law_issue: The dispute raised an issue arising from a public-law function of the authority.
predicates.authority_or_sale_process_challenged_for: A party challenged the authority’s jurisdiction or the sale process on grounds of lack of jurisdiction or abuse of authority.

issues.definition: When a writ proceeding concerns competing private property titles requiring proof of basic facts, raises no public-law issue, and does not challenge the authority or sale process for jurisdictional defect or abuse, the writ court should decline to adjudicate the private title dispute.
